title: The Case of the Wobbly Signs
markdown:
Nestled high in the Amberglow Mountains, where the air tasted like crisp apples and the sky wore its bluest cloak, lived a young ogre named Fernsnout. He was not the grumbling stomping sort of ogre you might imagine. Skin the colour of the softest moss. Eyes that darted with curiosity like busy summer berries. A heart as warm as a crackling hearth on a chilly evening. He was not alone in his happy little mountain home. He had a most special friend: a little rabbit with fur as fluffy as a dandelion seed-head and a tail that performed a constant joyful wiggle-dance. This dear companion was called Pipkin.

Fernsnout adored exploring. His very favourite place in all the wide world was the bluebell wood, a patch of ground where the tiny blue flowers carpeted the earth like a spilled pot of sapphires. He loved it best when the moon was a silvery coin in the inky sky, casting long dancing shadows. But lately something topsy-turvy had been happening in the bluebell wood. The important signposts, the ones that whispered the way to the Whispering Stream or the Sunny Meadow, were doing a jig. Sometimes they would point a friendly finger at a grumpy old toadstool that always grumbled about the dew, and other times they would aim straight for a particularly splashy puddle that giggled when you stepped in it.

“Someone is playing mischief with our signposts. And that simply will not do. I must discover who is doing such a thing.”

And so, one night, when the moonbeams were playing hide-and-seek through the leaves of the tall whispering trees, Fernsnout and Pipkin decided it was time. They set off on their moonlit adventure. The moonbeams dappled through the leaves, making the bluebells below twinkle and dance, like tiny happy stars that had fallen to the earth. Pipkin’s little tail gave an extra enthusiastic wag, a sure sign he was ready for whatever came next. “Are you ready for our adventure, Pipkin?” A low hum of delightful anticipation. Pipkin gave a little hop of agreement, his nose twitching.

They padded along a mossy path, following a signpost that usually pointed the way to the tinkling Whispering Stream. But tonight that very same signpost was tilted over, pointing with all its might toward a very old, very wise-looking oak tree. Fernsnout stroked his chin, eyes squinting slightly. As they tiptoed past the ancient oak, a tiny rustle, like the whisper of a butterfly’s wing, brushed against his ear. Then came the faint sweet scent of toasted marshmallows, and then a shimmering blur of colour darted from behind the roots.

Out from behind the gnarled roots peeked a most astonishing little creature. Scales that shimmered with all the colours of a rainbow caught in a sunbeam. Delicate wings that fluttered as gracefully as butterfly wings. A dragon hatchling, no bigger than Fernsnout’s favourite teddy bear. This tiny dragon, whose name Fernsnout would soon learn was Willowisp, gave a playful nudge to the wobbly signpost with her little nose, making it wobble even more. She let out a tiny puff of smoke that smelled delightfully of toasted marshmallows and warm honey.

Fernsnout could not help but beam. “Well, hello there, little one.” Willowisp blinked her big golden eyes, wide with wonder, and gave a happy little chirp. She nudged the signpost again, as if to say, look at me.

“Oh dear me.” A thoughtful look. “I think I am starting to understand who is moving our dear signposts.”

Just then a soft melodic voice drifted through the trees. “Hello there, Fernsnout. Is that you I hear?”

From behind a cluster of particularly tall and proud bluebells, a woman emerged. A face as kind as a warm hug, framed by wispy grey hair that seemed to catch the moonlight. She carried a large woven basket overflowing with the most wonderful smelling herbs: mint that tickled your nose, lavender that soothed your worries, and something sweet and comforting that smelled just like baking. This was Agnes, the kind witch of the bluebell wood.

“Agnes. We are trying to figure out why the signposts keep moving around. It is quite a mystery.”

Agnes smiled, her eyes crinkling at the corners. “Ah, yes. It seems young Willowisp here cannot quite see the signposts very well in the moonlight. When she tries to play and reach for things, she accidentally nudges them. She does not mean any harm at all, dear Fernsnout, but it does make things a bit confusing for travellers trying to find their way.”

Fernsnout looked over at Willowisp, who was now happily trying to catch a shimmering moonbeam with her tiny sparkling paw. His shoulders slumped slightly. He felt a little pang of sadness. He did not want anyone to get lost, especially not on such a beautiful moonlit night. “That is not good at all.” Pipkin, sensing Fernsnout’s gentle concern, nudged his leg with his soft head.

Agnes, with her wise eyes, noticed Fernsnout’s thoughtful frown. “Do not worry your mossy head. We can certainly fix this. I have just the thing in my basket.” With a little rustle and a clink she rummaged through her collection of herbs and pulled out a small wooden pot. Inside, something glowed with a soft gentle light. “This is glow-moss paste. It shines beautifully all through the night.”

Fernsnout’s eyes widened with wonder, and then a big bright idea sparked within him. “That is it. We can paint the signposts with the glow-moss paste. Then everyone will see them, even Willowisp.”

And so a wonderful plan was hatched. Fernsnout, Pipkin, and Agnes set to work with cheerful hearts. Willowisp, delighted to be part of the mission, carefully nudged the signposts into just the right position, her scales twinkling with excitement. Then Agnes and Fernsnout, with gentle hands, carefully painted each signpost with the magical glowing moss paste. Soon the signposts stood tall and proud, no longer wobbly, but shining with a soft friendly light that could be seen from far and wide in the moonlit wood. Willowisp chirped with pure happiness, and her rainbow scales seemed to sparkle even brighter.

“There. Now everyone will be able to find their way safely, and Willowisp can play to her heart’s content without any confusion.”

Fernsnout felt a warm happy feeling spread through him, like sunshine filling his chest. He had helped solve the mystery. Pipkin’s tail performed an extra-special triple-waggling dance of pure delight. “Thank you, Agnes. And thank you, Willowisp, for your help.”

As the moon climbed even higher, casting a soft glow over the now-bright signposts, Fernsnout and Pipkin began their happy journey home. The glowing signposts winked at them like friendly stars as they passed, guiding their way back to their cozy home in the Amberglow Mountains. Fernsnout snuggled into his soft warm bed, with Pipkin curled up like a furry little pillow at his feet, and drifted off to sleep. His dreams were filled with the gentle shimmer of moonbeams, and the signposts, still shining, kept pointing the right way.
characters: Fernsnout (young ogre who loves the bluebell wood), Pipkin (a rabbit with a wiggle-dance tail)
